content: 1. A study conducted in rural Malawi found that providing small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements to children did not significantly enhance their growth by 18 months of age. This was determined through a randomized controlled trial published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2015. 2. Research in rural Nepal assessed the effects of alternative maternal micronutrient supplements on low birth weight. This double-blind, randomized community trial, published in BMJ in 2003, highlighted the potential impact of such interventions on birth outcomes. 3. A study in Ghana demonstrated that lipid-based nutrient supplements increased the birth size of infants born to first-time mothers. This research, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2015, corresponds to findings from a Cochrane review study. 4. In Zimbabwe, a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial evaluated the effects of micronutrient supplementation on gestational length and birth size. The findings, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2004, provided insights into the role of maternal nutrition during pregnancy. 5. A study in rural Gambia explored the association between prenatal lipid-based nutritional supplementation and fetal growth. Published in Maternal and Child Nutrition in 2017, this research aligns with findings from a Cochrane review study. 6. A randomized trial in rural Bangladesh, known as the JiVitA-3 trial, compared the effects of maternal multiple micronutrient supplementation versus iron-folic acid supplementation on infant mortality and adverse birth outcomes. The results, published in JAMA in 2014, emphasized the potential benefits of comprehensive micronutrient interventions. 7. Research in Pakistan evaluated the comparative impact of multiple micronutrient and iron-folate supplementation during pregnancy on birth outcomes. Published in Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2009, the study highlighted the advantages of broader micronutrient supplementation. 8. A randomized controlled trial in Guinea-Bissau investigated the effects of prenatal multimicronutrient supplements on birth weight and perinatal mortality. The findings, published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2005, underscored the importance of maternal nutrition. 9. A double-blind randomized controlled trial in China assessed the impact of micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy on birth outcomes. Published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2013, the study provided evidence for the benefits of such interventions. 10. In Nepal, a randomized controlled trial examined the effects of antenatal micronutrient supplementation on birth weight and gestational duration. The results, published in The Lancet in 2005, highlighted the significance of maternal nutrition in improving neonatal outcomes. 11. A trial in rural Burkina Faso evaluated the effects of maternal multiple micronutrient supplementation on fetal growth. Published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2008, the study demonstrated the positive impact of comprehensive supplementation. 12. The SUMMIT study in Indonesia investigated the effect of maternal multiple micronutrient supplementation on fetal loss and infant death. This double-blind, cluster-randomized trial, published in The Lancet in 2008, provided critical insights into maternal and infant health. 13. A cluster-randomized controlled trial in West Java, Indonesia, assessed the role of maternal multiple micronutrient supplementation in preventing low birth weight. Published in Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2009, the study emphasized the importance of maternal nutrition programs. 14. The MINIMat study in Bangladesh evaluated the effects of prenatal food and micronutrient supplementation on infant development. Published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2008, the findings highlighted the long-term benefits of maternal nutrition interventions. 15. A programmatic study in rural Niger demonstrated that prenatal multiple micronutrient supplementation had a greater impact on birth weight than iron and folic acid supplementation. Published in Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2007, the study emphasized the importance of comprehensive maternal nutrition. 16. A trial in rural western China assessed the impact of micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy on birth weight, gestational duration, and perinatal mortality. Published in BMJ in 2008, the findings supported the use of multiple micronutrient interventions. 17. A meta-analysis of 17 randomized trials in lowand middle-income countries examined the modifiers of maternal multiple micronutrient supplementation on stillbirth, birth outcomes, and infant mortality. Published in The Lancet Global Health in 2017, the study provided robust evidence for the benefits of such interventions. 18. A 2019 publication in the Journal of Nutrition emphasized the need for updated WHO guidelines on multiple micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy, based on emerging evidence. 19. A study in Tanzania evaluated the effects of vitamin supplementation on perinatal outcomes among HIV-negative women. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2007, the research highlighted the role of vitamins in improving maternal and neonatal health. 20. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in BMC Medicine in 2016 explored the long-term health benefits of maternal antenatal multiple micronutrient supplementation for children. 21. Modeling results from three high-burden Asian countries demonstrated that multiple micronutrient supplements are more cost-effective than iron and folic acid supplementation. Published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2019, the study provided economic evidence for scaling up such interventions. 22. A cost-effectiveness analysis in Bangladesh and Burkina Faso highlighted the benefits of replacing iron-folic acid supplements with multiple micronutrient supplements for pregnant women. Published in Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences in 2019, the study emphasized the economic and health impacts of this transition. 23. A Cochrane review in 2017 summarized the evidence on multiple micronutrient supplementation during pregnancy, highlighting its benefits for maternal and neonatal health. 24. A 2018 publication in Value in Health discussed the appropriate use of cost-effectiveness analysis thresholds in lowand middle-income countries, emphasizing trends in cost-per-DALY studies. 25. A 2016 article in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization reviewed the pros and cons of cost-effectiveness thresholds, providing insights into their application in global health. 26. A 2018 publication in Maternal and Child Nutrition outlined considerations for the successful integration of multiple micronutrient supplements into routine antenatal care services, emphasizing quality and implementation strategies. 27. The WHO Steering Group and external experts contributed to the development of guidelines on maternal and perinatal health, ensuring evidence-based recommendations for global health practices.
